Dispatch
dis-PACH
v.t. (to finish or perform quickly; to put to death; to send off with speed)
Old French despeechier, from des-, undoing, and a root related to pied, foot, or to being caught — to free something from delay, sending it off quickly. In its harsher sense, the word narrowed to the quick ending of a life.

Biblical Definition

Ezekiel's allegory of the two adulterous sisters, Aholah and Aholibah, standing for Samaria and Jerusalem, reaches its judgment with a phrase whose violence is deliberate rather than incidental: the company shall stone them with stones, and dispatch them with their swords; they shall slay their sons and their daughters, and burn up their houses with fire. The dispatch named here is not a euphemism softening the judgment but its stated method, a quick, decisive killing that ends the allegory's long, patiently detailed description of covenant unfaithfulness in a single, unadorned act.

The chapter's closing purpose, stated immediately after, is not merely retributive: Thus will I cause lewdness to cease out of the land, that all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness. A dispatch this severe is presented as instructive as much as punitive, a public and final judgment meant to teach a wider audience the actual cost of the covenant-breaking the allegory has spent an entire chapter describing in uncomfortable detail. Scripture's willingness to record such a judgment without softening its language is itself part of the text's argument: a covenant taken as seriously as marriage, when broken as seriously as adultery, is not treated by the prophets as a matter to be described gently.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): to send off or execute with haste; also, to put to death, especially with quickness or without delay.

expand to see more

DISPATCH, v.t. To perform or send off quickly; also, to kill or put to death speedily.

COVENANT, n. A solemn agreement, especially between God and his people, often figured as a marriage.

LEWDNESS, n. Lustful, unchaste conduct; gross sexual immorality; in Scripture, often a figure for covenant unfaithfulness.

ALLEGORY, n. A figurative narrative in which characters and events represent abstract or spiritual truths.

JUDGMENT, n. The act of judging; a sentence pronounced, especially the divine sentence upon sin.

Key Scripture

Eze 23:46 — "For thus saith the Lord GOD; I will bring up a company upon them, and will give them to be removed and spoiled."

Eze 23:47 — "And the company shall stone them with stones, and dispatch them with their swords; they shall slay their sons and their daughters, and burn up their houses with fire."

Eze 23:48 — "Thus will I cause lewdness to cease out of the land, that all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness."

Eze 16:38 — "And I will judge thee, as women that break wedlock and shed blood are judged; and I will give thee blood in fury and jealousy."

Modern Corruption

Covenant unfaithfulness is treated as a private failing with limited consequence, when Ezekiel's allegory pictures its judgment in the same severe terms Scripture reserves for capital crimes, a dispatch meant to be publicly instructive, not merely privately regretted.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; to dispatch still means to finish, often violently, with speed. The principle worth recovering is why the prophets are willing to describe covenant-breaking in language this severe rather than softer, more clinical terms. Ezekiel judges the sisters as women that break wedlock and shed blood are judged, treating spiritual unfaithfulness with the same gravity Israel's law gave to adultery and bloodshed.

The stated purpose of the judgment, that all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness, refuses to let the dispatch be read as mere vengeance disconnected from any larger lesson. Scripture's severity here is not gratuitous; it is calibrated to match the seriousness of the covenant actually broken, and the text's own discomfort in the reader's ear is part of how seriously it wants covenant faithfulness to be taken in the first place.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew karath (H3772), to cut off, to dispatch by the sword; the verb behind “dispatch” in Ezekiel 23:47, the same root used of cutting a covenant.

expand to see more

Hebrew bathar or karath (H3772) — to cut off, to cut down; the verb underlying “dispatch,” the same root elsewhere used of cutting (making) a covenant.

Hebrew ragam (H7275) — to stone, to cast stones; the specific method of execution named alongside dispatch by the sword.

Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit fornication, to be a harlot; the standing verb for the covenant-breaking allegorized throughout Ezekiel 23.

Hebrew zimmah (H2154) — lewdness, wickedness, especially of a sexual nature; the word behind “lewdness” in Ezekiel 23:48.

Hebrew qana (H7065) — to be jealous, zealous; the covenant jealousy behind the judgment of Ezekiel 16:38.

Usage

"“the company shall stone them with stones, and dispatch them with their swords” — the judgment on covenant unfaithfulness."

"“that all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness” — the instructive purpose behind the severity."

"“I will judge thee, as women that break wedlock and shed blood are judged” — the same severity from Ezekiel sixteen."
